note: F1: the Key Fact repeated the same undercount.

find: Three ethical principles: informed consent (voluntary agreement after full information), confidentiality (protecting identifying information), harm to participants (minimising risk).

note: F1: the takeaway repeated the same undercount.

expect:
Mastering: Arguments supporting official statistics: large-scale, nationally consistent, free to access, allow long-term trend analysis; the Crime Survey for England and Wales provides data on millions of households. Arguments against: official statistics are limited by under-reporting (the dark figure of unrecorded crime); they are politically produced and may reflect government priorities rather than social reality; different perspectives interpret the same statistics differently (functionalist, Marxist and interactionist readings diverge). Qualitative methods (participant observation, unstructured interviews) may offer insight statistics obscure. The answer names at least two perspectives or contexts, uses sociological vocabulary (validity, reliability, dark figure), and reaches a supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides addressed; at least one named perspective or method cited; a judgement reached.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some concepts named; conclusion present but assertive.

Emerging: Basic description of statistics or methods; little evaluation; no clear judgement.
value:
Mastering: Arguments supporting official statistics: large-scale, nationally consistent, free to access, allow long-term trend analysis; the Crime Survey for England and Wales interviews about 31,000 adults a year and picks up crimes never reported to the police. Arguments against: official statistics are limited by under-reporting (the dark figure of unrecorded crime); they are politically produced and may reflect government priorities rather than social reality; different perspectives interpret the same statistics differently (functionalist, Marxist and interactionist readings diverge). Qualitative methods (participant observation, unstructured interviews) may offer insight statistics obscure. The answer names at least two perspectives or contexts, uses sociological vocabulary (validity, reliability, dark figure), and reaches a supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides addressed; at least one named perspective or method cited; a judgement reached.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some concepts named; conclusion present but assertive.

Emerging: Basic description of statistics or methods; little evaluation; no clear judgement.
note: F3: the CSEW interviews about 31,000 adults a year, not millions of households.
